newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - U.S. debt volatilities steady to firmer.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - U.S. debt volatilities steady to firmer.

text.p: Implied volatilities for U.S. fixed income options were mostly steady to firmer in late trade as the market remained cautious after Wednesday's sharp selloff in the underlying markets, dealers said.

Even though the underlying markets were relatively narrow-ranged today, growing concerns about a Federal Reserve rate hike after Fed chairman Alan Greenspan's hawkish remarks on Wednesday underpinned volatilities, they added.
Implied volatilities for CBOT April and June T-bond futures options were steady to marginally firmer, both at around 10.1 percent in mid-afternoon.
Traders noted the question now seemed to be when, rather than if, the Fed would make a move, given Greenspan's comments hinting at a pre-emptive tightening.
They said the market was likely to be very sensitive to major economic indicators due out in the coming weeks, especially the February employment report on March 7.

"He (Greenspan) has given everybody a clear warning that if we see a strong payroll number, the ground for a pre-emptive strike has been laid," said a T-bond trader for a brokerage house at the Chicago Board of Trade.
But the tendency of the T-bond options market to pump up implied volatility levels ahead of monthly employment reports seemed to have faded in recent months, he said.
"It looks like we're starting to lose the trend in that regard, and people are clearly a lot more hesitant to take long vol positions into these payroll data," he said.

"Quite a few people appeared to be taking short vol positions into the numbers (in the past few months) and they seemingly have done okay," he said, adding that this was even with no significant markups before the data.
Volatilities were also steady to firmer at the shorter end of the yield curve.
Although June Eurodollar futures appeared to have priced in a 25-basis-point rate hike by the end of first half 1997, trader expected back months to come under further pressure.
"It seems everyone is talking about the yield curve flattening now," a brokerage trader at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange said.
Implied volatility for September Eurodollar futures options was a touch firmer at around 14.0 percent.
